Threads — manufacturing limits & gauge verification

Two different sets of numbers for two different jobs: manufacturing limits judge the part you make; gauge limits judge the gauge itself. Pick the thread, then choose the view.

Identify a thread from measurements

Measured a thread you don't recognise? Enter what you measured and the finder lists the standard threads whose limits fit, then near misses. Diameter alone is often ambiguous — add the pitch (thread gauge or count threads over 1 in) to narrow it to one.

Custom sizes are calculated from the standard's own formulas and are labelled “calculated” in the results — catalogue sizes above use the published tables.

Hydraulic ports — O-ring boss, flange & cavity

A port leaks at the seal, not the thread: the chamfer diameter, chamfer depth and angle squeeze the O-ring, and the spotface gives the fitting something square to seat on. Inspect those, not just the thread.

Which port do I have?

SAE ORB (J1926-1): UN / UNF thread, 12° or 15° O-ring chamfer at the mouth, flat spotface. Dash size = tube OD in 1/16 in (−8 = 1/2 in tube = 3/4-16).
ISO 6149-1: metric M thread with a 12° / 15° O-ring chamfer; may carry a raised identification ridge on the spotface.
BSPP (ISO 1179-1): G thread (55° form), flat spotface, no chamfer — the seal is a bonded washer or O-ring on the fitting face.
4-bolt flange (J518 / ISO 6162): plain bore with four tapped holes in a rectangle — measure the long and short hole spacing; Code 62 is the bigger pattern for the same size.
NPT / NPTF: tapered thread, no spotface seal — seals on the thread.
Use the thread finder in Threads to identify the thread first, then pick the port here.

Seal glands — O-ring groove check & design

An O-ring seals because it is squeezed. Too little squeeze leaks; too much wears, sets and won't assemble; a full gland has nowhere to swell; a big gap lets pressure push the ring out. This checks all four at the worst-case tolerance stack.

Learn — what each number means

Gland depth (L) — the radial space the ring is squeezed into: bore − groove Ø, divided by 2 (piston) or groove Ø − rod, divided by 2 (rod). It already includes the running clearance.
Squeeze — how much thinner the ring is made: (cross-section − L) ÷ cross-section. It is the seal. Below ≈ .007 in it can leak at low pressure; dynamic seals run about 10–16 % so they slide without tearing; static seals take up to 30 %.
Stretch — a piston ring is stretched onto its groove. Stretch thins the cross-section (Parker's curve: 5 % stretch ≈ 3.4 % thinner), which lowers squeeze — that is why this tool uses the stretched cross-section. Over 5 % ages the ring faster.
OD compression (rod) — a rod ring is pushed into its housing groove; a little OD interference holds it, too much makes it twist and roll.
Gland fill — ring area ÷ groove area. Rubber is incompressible: it needs room to swell in oil and expand with heat. Aim 60–85 %; never above 90 %.
Diametral clearance (E) — the gap the ring has to bridge. Pressure pushes rubber into it: the bigger the gap, the higher the pressure or the softer the ring, the sooner it extrudes (nibbled, "chewed" edges on the low-pressure side). Back-up rings close that door at high pressure.
Worst case — every result is shown at both tolerance extremes: smallest ring in the biggest groove (least squeeze) and biggest ring in the smallest groove (most squeeze, most fill).

Typical failures you can read from these numbers: leak at low pressure → squeeze too low; flat-sided ring (compression set) → squeeze too high or heat; nibbled edge → gap too big for the pressure; twisted / spiral cut ring in a dynamic gland → too much stretch, rough finish or a too-wide groove; cut at assembly → sharp edges, no lead-in chamfer.

Gland design values: Parker O-Ring Handbook ORD 5700, Design Chart 4-1 (industrial static) and 5-2 (industrial reciprocating) — gland depth and squeeze ranges confirmed identical in Global O-Ring & Seal's published tables. Cross-section reduction from stretch: Parker Figure 3-3 equations, which reproduce Freudenberg (FST) AS568 guide table values. Limits: Parker §3.5–3.7 (stretch ≤ 5 %, squeeze ≥ .007 in, dynamic ≈ 16 % max, static 30 % max, fill 60–85 %, ≥ 10 % void). AS568 sizes: Apple Rubber and Greene Tweed charts agree on 341 of 345 sizes; −391 ID (21.955, the other source's 21.995 breaks the series), −102 ID tol (.004 / .005 → .005 used) and −469 / −470 ID tol (.090 / .095 → .095 used) resolved toward the wider tolerance. Reference only — the seal maker's recommendation governs for critical applications.

Fits — ISO 286 hole & shaft limits

A fit is two tolerances meeting: the hole's band and the shaft's band. Where they sit relative to each other decides whether the parts slide, locate, or have to be pressed.

Learn — reading a fit

Capital letter = hole, small letter = shaft. The letter is where the band sits (H holes start at the nominal size and go up; h shafts start at nominal and go down; a–g shafts sit below nominal → clearance; k–p sit above → grip). The number is the IT grade — how wide the band is (IT6 ≈ ground, IT7 ≈ fine-turned / reamed, IT8–9 ≈ turned / bored, IT11 ≈ rough).
Clearance fit: the smallest hole is still bigger than the biggest shaft — always slides. Interference fit: the biggest hole is still smaller than the smallest shaft — must be pressed or shrunk. Transition: depends which parts meet — may slide, may need a tap.
Hole basis (H hole, choose the shaft letter) is the usual system: holes are made with fixed reamers and gauges, shafts are easy to turn to any size.
Inspect it right: a GO / NO-GO plug or ring at the two limits checks the band; a single measurement checks one point only — on round parts, out-of-roundness can pass a two-point check and still not assemble.

Built from ISO 286-1 base tables (standard tolerance grades IT4–IT11 and fundamental deviations d e f g h js k m n p, holes by the ISO 286-1 rules incl. Δ and the M6 250–315 special case). Checked cell-by-cell against a published ISO 286-2 table: 591 of 594 limits agree; the 3 that don't are typos in that table (each band's width disagrees with its own IT grade — f6 120–180, E7 315–400, K6 6–10). Common fits: the ISO preferred hole-basis fits. Reference only — ISO 286-2 governs.

General tolerances — ISO 2768

When a drawing dimension has no tolerance of its own, the title-block note sets it. "ISO 2768-mK" means class m for sizes and angles (Part 1) and class K for form and orientation (Part 2). Enter the size, pick the classes, and read the limits.

Full tables — ISO 2768-1 (f m c v) and ISO 2768-2 (H K L)
Learn — reading a general-tolerance note

Only untoleranced features. A dimension with its own tolerance, a basic (boxed) dimension, or a reference (bracketed) dimension is not covered.
Over the general tolerance is not automatic rejection — ISO 2768-1 says a part outside a general tolerance should only be rejected if its function is impaired. Your customer's agreement or drawing can say otherwise.
Part 2 does not cover cylindricity, profile of any line or surface, angularity, coaxiality, position or total run-out.
"-E" on the end (e.g. ISO 2768-mK-E) adds the envelope requirement to every single feature of size.
Status: ISO 2768-1:1989 is still current. ISO 2768-2:1989 was withdrawn and replaced by ISO 22081:2021, which has no H/K/L classes — but H/K/L notes are still on many drawings in use, and they mean these values.

ISO 2768-1:1989 Tables 1–3 and ISO 2768-2:1989 Tables 1–4. Every cell checked 2026-11-21 against the standards' own preview text and at least one independent reproduction (Wevolver transcription; Starrapid, camcut and University of Wisconsin metrology sheets). Where a reproduction disagreed (one prints ±0°20′ for class c, 120–400 mm), the standard's own text was used (±0°15′). Status: ISO 22081:2021 replaced ISO 2768-2 (ISO catalogue).

Surface finish — Ra, N-grades & cut-off

Turn a drawing callout into numbers you can check: Ra in µm or µin, the old ISO N-grade, and the cut-off (λc) and evaluation length to set on the profilometer.

Full tables — N-grades and cut-off selection
Setting up a Mitutoyo Surftest for an accurate reading

1. Choose the cut-off. Use the drawing's cut-off if it states one. Otherwise estimate the value, read λc from the result above, measure, and check that the measured value falls in the same row; if it does not, change λc to the row of the measured value and measure again (ISO 4288 procedure).
2. Set the conditions: λc (cut-off), sampling lengths ×5, λs as shown, Gaussian filter (the ISO 16610-21 filter; use 2CR75 or PC75 only when the drawing or customer asks for them), and the parameter the drawing calls for.
3. Stylus: the 2 µm, 60° stylus (0.75 mN) for λc up to 0.8 mm; the 5 µm, 90° stylus (4 mN) is acceptable for λc 2.5 mm, or whenever Ra is over 0.5 µm or Rz over 3 µm.
4. Measure across the lay (at right angles to the feed or grinding marks), on a clean surface, with the detector level to the surface and enough length for the traverse shown. If the surface is too short, reduce the number of sampling lengths and record that on the report (Mitutoyo Bulletin 2229, tip 1).
5. Check the instrument on its roughness specimen before use, and calibrate the stylus with the supplied specimen when the reading is off its certified value.
6. Judge the result. Parameters without "max" use the 16 % rule: if the first reading is below 70 % of the limit, the surface complies; otherwise take two more, and if all three are below the limit it complies; otherwise take nine more, and it complies if no more than two of the twelve exceed the limit. Parameters with "max" (e.g. Rz1max): measure at three or more places where the highest values are expected; no reading may exceed the limit.

Learn — Ra, Rz and the cut-off

Ra is the average height of the profile from its mean line. Rz is the average peak-to-valley height over the sampling lengths. They measure different things, so there is no fixed Ra ⇄ Rz conversion — any ratio you see is a rule of thumb for one kind of surface. If the drawing says Rz, measure Rz.
Cut-off λc is the filter that separates roughness from waviness, and it equals the sampling length. The wrong cut-off gives a different Ra on the same part — so when two people disagree on a finish, check the cut-off first.
Turned or ground surfaces with a regular feed mark are periodic: choose the cut-off from RSm (the mark spacing, roughly the feed). Most other surfaces are aperiodic: choose from Ra or Rz.
µin conversion: 1 µin = 0.0254 µm exactly. The N-grade table pairs each Ra in µm with a rounded µin value (0.8 µm ↔ 32 µin; exactly it is 31.5).

N-grades: ISO 1302:1978 Table 1 (preview text), matched by Machinery's Handbook 31st ed. Table 4 and Ceratizit / Xometry tables. Cut-off selection: ISO 4288:1996 rules as reproduced by Carl Zeiss "Surface parameters" (citing ISO 4288) and Machinery's Handbook 31st ed. Table 3 — every row agrees. Status (ISO catalogue): ISO 4288 withdrawn, revised by ISO 21920-3:2021; ISO 1302 replaced by ISO 21920-1:2021, which drops N-grades. Checked 2026-11-21. Traverse length, λs and stylus radius per cut-off, the 16 % and max rules: Mitutoyo Bulletin 2229 "Quick Guide to Surface Roughness Measurement" and the Mitutoyo catalogue "Quick Guide to Precision Measuring Instruments — Surftest" (ISO 3274 / JIS B 0651 table), which agree with each other and with ISO 4288. SJ-210 cut-off, λs and stylus options from the Mitutoyo SJ-210 specification. Checked 2026-11-22.

Fitting torque — JIC, ORFS, O-ring boss, ISO 6149, flanges, NPTF

Pick the connection and size to get the tightening torque (or flats / turns), what it means, and where the number comes from. Fitting makers publish different values for the same size, so the fitting maker's own table always governs. Use these when you don't have it.

Full tables — every size
Learn — why the numbers differ, flats vs torque, +10 % / −0

Why makers disagree: SAE J514 and J1453 set the joint geometry. Where SAE and ISO give a torque, it is a qualification test torque, the torque at which the joint must pass its tests. Each fitting maker then publishes its own assembly torques for its plating, lubrication and design. For example, Parker's ORFS assembly torques are higher than the SAE J1453 test torques. So when the fitting maker's table is available, use it.
Flats from finger tight: tighten the nut by hand until it stops, then turn it the stated number of hex flats with a wrench (one flat = 1/6 turn). For flare fittings Parker recommends this over torque, because plating and lubrication change how much clamp a given torque produces.
+10 % / −0: the value shown is the minimum. Tighten to at least that value, and no more than 10 % above it.
Two wrenches: hold the fitting body with a backup wrench while you tighten the nut, so the torque goes into the joint and doesn't twist the hose, tube or port.

Welding symbols — read one, build one

Set the parts of the symbol from the drawing. The tool draws it the AWS A2.4 way and says in plain words what the welder has to do.

ItemAWS A2.4 (North America)ISO 2553 system A
Arrow side / other sideOne solid line. Below = arrow side, above = other sideA solid line plus a dashed line. On the solid line = arrow side, on the dashed line = other side. The dashed line can be above or below
Fillet sizeBare number = leg sizeLetter in front: a = throat, z = leg (a5 ≈ z7)

ISO 2553 system B uses one line like AWS (below = arrow side). The title block or notes should say which system the drawing uses. A common error: reading an ISO "a6" fillet (6 mm throat, about 8.5 mm leg) as a 6 mm leg gives an undersized weld.

Visual weld inspection — AWS D1.1 accept / reject

Enter what you measured. Each check shows the D1.1 Table 8.1 limit (nontubular connections) and passes or rejects. Leave a check blank to skip it. Check that D1.1 is the right code first — see "Which code applies?" below.

Always

Fillet size and profile

Undercut

Piping porosity

How to inspect a weld visually — step by step

1. Before welding: check the fit-up against the drawing and WPS: joint type, root opening, bevel angle, alignment, and clean metal (no mill scale, oil, paint or moisture in the joint). A bad fit-up can't be fixed by welding over it.
2. When to inspect: D1.1 lets visual inspection start once the weld has cooled to ambient temperature. For ASTM A514, A517 and A709 HPS 100W steels it must wait at least 48 hours after welding, because delayed (hydrogen) cracks can appear late.
3. Light and access: good light, clean weld (slag and spatter removed), a magnifier for suspected cracks.
4. Look first: cracks (any crack rejects), lack of fusion at the toes, unfilled craters, overlap (weld metal rolled over the base metal without fusing), arc strikes, porosity.
5. Then measure: fillet size with a fillet gauge (on a convex fillet the gauge checks the leg; on a concave fillet it checks the throat, which is what governs a concave weld); undercut depth with an undercut or bridge cam gauge; convexity and reinforcement with a bridge cam gauge or a straight edge and feeler; length and spacing of intermittent welds with a rule.
6. Record what you found, where, and the result. A reject is repaired (by the WPS) and re-inspected.

What each discontinuity is

Crack — a fracture in the weld or heat-affected zone, the most serious defect.
Incomplete fusion — weld metal not melted into the base metal or the previous pass.
Incomplete joint penetration — the weld doesn't reach through the joint where full penetration was asked for.
Undercut — a groove melted into the base metal along the toe and left unfilled.
Overlap — weld metal lying on the base metal past the toe without fusing to it.
Porosity — gas pores; "piping" porosity is elongated and runs into the weld.
Crater — the dip left where the arc stopped; an unfilled crater often has a crack.
Undersized weld — leg or throat smaller than the drawing.
Excess convexity / reinforcement — too much weld metal built up on the face, which concentrates stress at the toes.

Which code applies?

The drawing, PO or customer specification decides — this tool uses AWS D1.1 (structural steel) because it is the most widely used North American code. Others you may meet: AWS D14.4 (welded joints in machinery and equipment), ASME Section IX (welder and procedure qualification for pressure equipment), and ISO 5817 quality levels B / C / D on European drawings. If the drawing names no code, ask before you accept or reject, and record what you used.
Edition matters: D1.1:2025 clarified the undercut and porosity rows. It added pro-rated limits for welds shorter than 12 in, which this tool does not apply. Check the edition named in your contract.

Symbols: AWS A2.4 conventions as given by several independent references that agree (Draftsperson, clause5.io, Welders Supply, Weld Fab World); ISO 2553 differences per TWI, Welding Australia (AS 1101.3) and others. Acceptance: AWS D1.1/D1.1M Table 8.1, from a reproduction of the 2020 table and summaries of the 2020 and 2025 tables that agree on every value used. Convexity: Table 7.9 Schedule C (clause5.io, PDHonline M381, ESAB). Butt reinforcement: only the base-metal ≤ 1 in row (1/8 in). Tubular connections are not covered.

Plain GO / NO-GO gauges — sizes and class

Enter the hole or pin limits from the drawing. The tool gives the GO and NO-GO gauge sizes, which way the gauge tolerance goes, and a gauge-maker class that keeps the gauges within about 10 % of the part tolerance.

Gauge-maker tolerance chart (ASME B89.1.5 basis)

Class tolerances: gauge-maker charts per ASME B89.1.5 — Meyer Gage and Fox Valley Metrology publish identical inch and metric charts (Judge / Glastonbury Southern, Vermont Gage and others agree on the rows they show). Tolerance direction: plug GO plus, NO-GO minus; ring GO minus, NO-GO plus (Meyer, Fox Valley). 10 % rule: Vermont Gage and Judge Tool. Thread gauges are in Threads → Gauge verification.

Thread gauges and their masters — metric (ISO 1502) and inch (ASME B1.2)

Choose the thread. The tool gives the pitch-diameter limits for the GO and NOGO thread plugs and rings (new and worn), and for the check plugs and setting plugs used to verify ring gauges, calculated by ISO 1502 for metric threads and taken from ASME B1.2 for inch threads. Use the numbers to check gauges at calibration and to order master gauges.

Full thread dimensions (major, minor, tap drill) are in Threads.

Calibration guide — thread plug, ring and check plug gauges

1. Before measuring

  • Measure at the reference temperature of 20 °C (ISO 1). Let gauges and masters soak in the measuring room until they reach room temperature; a steel gauge grows about 11.5 µm per metre per °C.
  • Clean the gauge, then inspect the threads under magnification for burrs, nicks, corrosion and damaged crests. A damaged gauge is withdrawn whatever its size.
  • Confirm the identification (size, pitch, class, GO / NOGO, serial number) against the calibration record.

2. Thread plug gauges (GO and NOGO) — measured directly

  • Major diameter: measure with a bench micrometer or a length-measuring machine set on gauge blocks, at several positions along the thread, and compare with the major-diameter limits in this tool (GO plug: min–max; NOGO plug: nominal, tolerance from the certificate).
  • Pitch diameter: measure over three wires (see the calculator below) and convert to the simple pitch diameter. Compare with the limits in this tool: a new gauge must lie within its new limits; a used GO or NOGO plug is withdrawn when its pitch diameter is below its wear limit.
  • Pitch and flank angles: checked when a gauge is new or repaired, on an optical or contact thread-measuring machine; routine recalibration normally repeats major and pitch diameter only, plus the visual check.
  • Reference procedure: VDI/VDE/DGQ 2618 Part 4.8 (setting plugs, thread plug gauges and check plugs).

3. Thread ring gauges — verified with check plugs

  • The pitch diameter of a small ring cannot be measured directly. ISO 1502 verifies a solid ring with screw check plugs made to the limits in this tool: a new GO ring passes when the GO-GO check plug (TT) screws through and the GO-NOGO check plug (TZ) enters by no more than one turn.
  • In service, the GO ring is withdrawn when its wear check plug (TS) enters by more than one turn. The NOGO ring works the same way with ZT, ZZ and ZS. The one turn is counted when the check plug is withdrawn (ISO 1502, quoted in IS 2334).
  • Adjustable rings are set to their setting plug, locked and sealed, then checked with the wear check plug in service.
  • Larger rings can also be measured directly on a thread-measuring machine or scanner; the certificate then reports the pitch diameter itself.
  • Check plugs and setting plugs are calibrated like thread plug gauges (major and pitch diameter by the three-wire method) against their limits in this tool.
  • Reference procedure: VDI/VDE/DGQ 2618 Part 4.9 (setting rings and thread ring gauges).
  • Inch (UN) rings, ASME B1.2: there are no check plugs. The GO ring is set to, and checked on, its GO setting plug; the LO ring on its LO setting plug. The setting plugs are the masters you calibrate.

4. Records, interval and traceability

  • ISO 9001:2015 clause 7.1.5.2: gauges are calibrated against standards traceable to national or international standards, identified with their calibration status, and protected from adjustment and damage. If a gauge is found out of tolerance, review the parts it accepted since the last good calibration.
  • Use a laboratory accredited to ISO/IEC 17025 for the masters (check plugs, setting plugs, wires). The certificate should report measured values and the measurement uncertainty; set the accept / reject decision rule with the uncertainty (ILAC-G8).
  • Set the interval from use and history, not one fixed number; ILAC-G24 describes the methods. Shorten it when a gauge is found worn or damaged, lengthen it when several calibrations show little change.
  • Record for every gauge: identification, values measured, limits used (new and wear), result, date, next due date, who calibrated it and which masters were used.

5. Three-wire pitch diameter

For a 60° thread: simple pitch diameter E = M − 3w + 0.866025·P, where M is the measurement over the wires and w the wire diameter. The best wire size is w = 0.57735·P. Accredited laboratories also correct for lead angle and wire contact force; this calculator omits those corrections, so use the laboratory's corrected value for acceptance.

Method: ISO 1502:1996 (identical to GB/T 3934-2003 and to the IS 2334:2001 reprint). Gauge tolerances TR, TPL, TCP, m, ZR, ZPL from Table 4, two sources (GB/T 3934 and IS 2334). Wear allowances from GB/T 3934. Plug limits reproduce the RP-Kalibrierlabor M10×1.5-6G and Stille M45×2-6G calibration certificates exactly; ring, check-plug, wear-check-plug and setting-plug limits reproduce ISO 6698 Table 4 (hub thread 6g, calculated by its authors with the ISO 1502 formulas) and the iCAD ISO 1502 calculator example for M10-6g, every value. Workpiece limits from the ISO 965-1 tables (see Threads). Tested in tests/mgauge.test.js.

More MSA — Type 1, bias & linearity, attribute agreement

Gage R&R asks "do people and repeats agree?". These ask the other questions an auditor asks: is the gauge itself capable, is it accurate across its range, and do inspectors make the same good / bad call?

Learn — which study, and what passes

Type 1 (VDA 5 / Bosch booklet 10, Minitab method): one operator measures one reference part 25–50 times. Cg = 0.2·T ÷ 6s compares the gauge's scatter with 20 % of the tolerance; Cgk also subtracts the bias. Both ≥ 1.33 is the common acceptance. Run it before a Gage R&R — a gauge that fails here can't pass R&R.
Bias & linearity (AIAG MSA 4th ed.): bias = average reading − true value. Measure 5+ masters across the range; if bias changes with size, the gauge is non-linear. Look at the slope: if its t-test is significant (p < 0.05) linearity is a problem; if the bias-at-each-reference or the intercept is significant, there is a bias problem. %Linearity = |slope| × 100.
Attribute agreement (AIAG): for go / no-go and visual calls. Kappa is agreement corrected for luck: 1 = perfect, 0 = no better than guessing. AIAG: > 0.75 good, < 0.40 poor. Effectiveness = share of parts called right every time (≥ 90 % acceptable); miss rate = bad parts passed (≤ 2 %); false alarm = good parts rejected (≤ 5 %).

Formulas: Type 1 per Minitab's Type 1 gage study method (K = 20 %, L = 6, the VDA 5 / Bosch booklet 10 basis). Bias & linearity per AIAG MSA 4th edition (§III-B); the worked example is the AIAG / Minitab linearity data set and this tool reproduces its published slope (−0.13167), intercept (0.73667) and R² (71.4 %). Kappa: Cohen (two ratings) and Fleiss (many ratings) — tested on the standard published examples (κ = 0.40 and κ = 0.210). Acceptance guidance: AIAG MSA 4th ed. Tested in tests/msa.test.js.

Cylinder & oil — force, speed, rod buckling, tube stress, ISO 4406

Quick engineering checks for a hydraulic cylinder: what it pushes and pulls, how fast it moves, whether the rod buckles, whether the tube holds the pressure — and what the oil cleanliness code means.

Rod buckling (push)

Yield strengths: look your grade up in Materials Atlas (min yield, the right condition).

ISO 4406 cleanliness code

Learn — what these checks mean

Force = pressure × area. Extending, pressure acts on the full bore; retracting, only on the annulus (bore area − rod area) — so a cylinder always pulls weaker and retracts faster.
Buckling — a long, thin rod pushing a load fails sideways long before the steel yields. The column length is pin-to-pin (or mount-to-load) fully extended; the end fixity multiplies it (K). Slender rods follow Euler; short, stocky rods follow Johnson (yield matters). A safety factor of 3–4 on buckling is common practice for cylinders.
Tube hoop stress — pressure tries to burst the tube. Barlow (thin wall, uses OD) is the quick check; Lamé (thick wall) gives the true peak at the bore surface, which is what matters for thick tubes.
ISO 4406 — three numbers for particles ≥ 4 / 6 / 14 µm per mL. Each step up doubles the particle count, so 19/17/14 is roughly twice as dirty as 18/16/13. Typical targets: servo / proportional valves 16/14/11 or cleaner, general industrial hydraulics 18/16/13–19/17/14 — check the component maker's requirement.

Formulas: area / force / speed — fluid power basics; buckling — Euler and J. B. Johnson column equations with effective-length factor K (theoretical values; Machinery's Handbook / Shigley); tube — Barlow and Lamé thick-wall equations. ISO 4406 scale numbers 0–28: Petro-Canada's ISO 4406:1999 table and an independent particle-count guide agree on every code. Reference only — design to your cylinder standard (NFPA / ISO 6020 / 6022) and the customer's spec.

GD&T helpers & measurement uncertainty

Bonus tolerance, virtual condition and fastener formulas (ASME Y14.5) — and a GUM uncertainty budget so you know how big a measurement's ± really is.

One line per source: name, value, type, sensitivity — type = normal k (e.g. normal 2 for a calibration certificate's U), rect (± half-width, e.g. resolution/2, spec limits), tri, u (U-shaped), or typeA n (value = std dev of n repeat readings). Sensitivity defaults to 1.

Learn — bonus, virtual condition, uncertainty

MMC = the size with the most material (smallest hole, largest pin). With Ⓜ, the stated position tolerance applies at MMC; as the feature departs toward LMC it gains bonus tolerance equal to that departure — that's why a hole that measures bigger is allowed to be further off position.
Virtual condition — the worst-case boundary the mating part must clear (hole: MMC − tolerance; pin: MMC + tolerance). It is what a functional gauge pin / ring is made to. Resultant condition — the other extreme, used for wall-thickness and minimum-material checks.
Fasteners: floating (clearance holes in both parts) T = H − F; fixed (one part threaded / press-fit) T₁ + T₂ = H − F — split between the parts, often equally.
Uncertainty (GUM): turn every error source into a standard uncertainty (rectangular ÷ √3, triangular ÷ √6, U-shaped ÷ √2, certificate U ÷ k, repeatability s ÷ √n), multiply by its sensitivity, add in quadrature (root-sum-square), then × k (2 ≈ 95 %). Rule of thumb: the expanded uncertainty should be ≤ 1/4 – 1/10 of the tolerance (TUR 4:1 – 10:1). Near a limit, ISO 14253-1 says conformance is only proven inside the tolerance shrunk by U.

GD&T: ASME Y14.5-2018 definitions of MMC, LMC, bonus tolerance, virtual and resultant condition; floating / fixed fastener formulas per Y14.5 Appendix B. Position from coordinates: Ø = 2√(Δx² + Δy²). Uncertainty: JCGM 100 (GUM) — divisors √3 / √6 / √2, quadrature sum, expanded U = k·uc; decision rule ISO 14253-1. Tested in tests/cyl-gdt.test.js.

Add the dimensions that build the gap, in order. Direction + means a bigger dimension makes the gap bigger; − means it makes the gap smaller.

EXAMPLE DATA — demonstration only, not real measurements.

Assembly gap

Worst-case is a guarantee: if every part is within its own tolerance, the assembly gap stays inside these limits.

RSS is a prediction, not a guarantee: it assumes each process is centred, normal, and independent, with each tolerance equal to ±3σ.

Sigma ⇄ PPM — capability in plain numbers

Convert between Cpk, expected defects (PPM) and yield. With the shift off, the process is treated as centred and PPM counts both spec tails. With the shift on, the Motorola 1.5σ-shift convention applies and the result is quoted as DPMO (one tail) — the convention behind "6 sigma = 3.4 DPMO".

Equivalent values

True position — with MMC / LMC bonus

Enter how far the measured feature centre sits from its true (basic) position, the stated position tolerance, and the feature's actual mating size. Bonus tolerance is how far the actual size has departed from the MMC (or LMC) size limit.

Bonus is earned only while the measured size is inside its limits, moving away from the modifier limit (Ⓜ: toward LMC; Ⓛ: toward MMC). A size beyond the modifier limit — or beyond the other limit, when you enter it — is out of size: no bonus and no PASS.

Result

What this means: the diametral deviation 2√(Δx² + Δy²) is the diameter of the smallest zone around true position that contains the measured centre; it must fit inside the stated tolerance plus any bonus the feature's size has earned.

Geometry per ASME Y14.5 — exact diametral deviation, no statistical assumptions. All values in the same unit (mm or in) as entered.

Short-run & batch production

When part numbers change every few hours, study the machine and the feature, not the part number.

PRE-Control: approve a setup on the first few parts, with no history needed. Green is the middle half of the tolerance, yellow the outer quarters, red outside the spec.

Put different part numbers on one chart by plotting how far each reading is from the middle of its own tolerance. Use it per machine and feature type, e.g. "bores on Mill 3".

Learn — what the numbers mean and what to do next

Short, practical notes behind each tool. Thresholds are the ones this app uses, from the AIAG SPC and MSA reference manuals and ANSI/ASQ Z1.4.

Control limits are not spec limits

Control limits (UCL/LCL) come from your own data: the process average ± 3σ within. They tell you whether the process is stable. Spec limits (LSL/USL) come from the drawing. They tell you whether parts are acceptable.

A point can be in control and out of spec (a stable process that is not capable), or out of control and still in spec (something changed; find it before it makes scrap).

Do next: never move control limits to match the spec, and never adjust the machine for a point that is inside the control limits. That is tampering, and it adds variation.

The signals the SPC tool flags
  • Beyond a control limit: one point outside UCL/LCL.
  • Run of 8: eight points in a row on one side of the centre line (the average has shifted).
  • Trend of 6: six points in a row steadily rising or falling (tool wear, temperature, drift).

Do next: find and remove the special cause (tool change, new lot, new operator, setup) before you quote a Cpk. Capability from an unstable process does not predict tomorrow's parts.

Reading Cp, Cpk, Pp and Ppk
  • Cp: could the spread fit inside the tolerance if it were centred? Uses σ within.
  • Cpk: does it fit, given where the process actually sits? Uses σ within and the nearer spec limit.
  • Pp / Ppk: the same two ideas using σ overall (sample standard deviation), so they include drift between parts.
CpkThis app saysTypical action
≥ 1.33CapableMaintain control; reduce inspection only if the customer agrees.
1.00 – 1.33MarginalCapable today, little margin for drift. Watch closely; plan an improvement.
< 1.00Not capableExpect defects. Contain (100 % inspection or sort), then fix the process.

Cp much higher than Cpk (gap of 0.3 or more): the spread is fine but the process is off-centre. Recentring is usually the cheapest fix.
Cp low too: the spread itself is too wide. Reduce variation, or review the tolerance with design.

Sample size matters. With 30 values, a calculated Cpk of 1.33 could plausibly be anywhere from about 1.0 to 1.7 (95 % confidence). Quote capability from more data when the decision matters; many customers ask for at least 100 values or 25 subgroups.

Cpk and PPM assume roughly normal data. Check the shape in Data Check first.

Normality (Data Check)

The Anderson–Darling test asks whether the data could reasonably come from a normal distribution. A p-value below 0.05 means probably not normal.

Do next: look at the histogram. Two humps usually means two streams mixed (two machines, two cavities, two operators): split them. A long tail on one side is common for flatness, runout, position and roughness, which cannot go below zero. Then normal-based PPM is unreliable; report the observed out-of-spec count instead.

Gage R&R: can you trust the measurement?
%GRRAIAG verdict
< 10 %Acceptable
10 – 30 %May be acceptable, depending on how important the feature is and the cost of a better gauge
> 30 %Not acceptable: improve the measurement system

% of tolerance judges the gauge for accepting parts. % of study variation judges it for process control. ndc (number of distinct categories) should be 5 or more.

Do next: high EV (repeatability) points at the gauge or fixture: clamping, wear, resolution. High AV (reproducibility) points at people or method: write a clearer procedure and train. Use parts that cover the real process range; ten near-identical parts make any gauge look bad on % study variation.

AQL sampling: what acceptance does and doesn't mean

AQL is the worst process average that is still acceptable over many lots. It is not a promise about any one lot: a lot that passes can still contain defectives.

Look up the code letter from lot size and inspection level (General II is the normal default), then the sample size n and the accept (Ac) and reject (Re) numbers. Accept the lot if defectives found ≤ Ac; reject if ≥ Re.

This app shows normal inspection. Z1.4 also has tightened and reduced inspection with switching rules; apply them if your contract uses them.

Pareto, True Position and Stack-Up in one line each
  • Pareto: fix the few biggest bars first. "80/20" is a rule of thumb, not a law; rank by cost or severity too, not only count.
  • True Position: position = 2 × √(Δx² + Δy²), compared with the diameter tolerance zone. At MMC the zone grows by how far the feature has departed from MMC (the bonus).
  • Stack-Up: worst case adds every tolerance and always holds. RSS assumes centred, normal, independent processes and gives a tighter but statistical prediction.
